title: Casimir (4 March)
hookLine: a young Polish prince who turned back from a war and gave to the poor

lines: A YOUNG PRINCE AT THE HEAD OF AN ARMY.
cards: A young prince rides at the head of an army. His father, the king of Poland, has sent him to take a neighboring crown, the crown of Hungary, which some nobles there have offered him.
Banners, horses, the whole weight of a dynasty behind him. And partway there, the prince turns around and goes home.

Tradition gives more than one reason: soldiers deserting for lack of pay, a pope against the war, a rival king already holding the throne. But the Church remembers what the prince did with that moment.

teach.h: A PRINCE WHO WON'T MARCH AGAIN.
teach.b: The story goes that his father was furious and sent him away from court for a while. Casimir would not be talked into marching again.
Whatever the full mix of reasons, his biographers tell it as a matter of conscience, and he never changed his mind. What he did instead is the part they lingered on.
He lived plainly inside a palace.

Tradition says he slept on the floor, rose at night to pray at church doors before they opened, and gave his own money to the poor, the sick and pilgrims, so freely that he became known as their defender.
He loved Mary deeply, and tradition says he loved a Latin hymn that begins Omni die dic Mariae, daily, daily, sing to Mary, and that a copy was buried with him.
He fell ill with a lung disease and died young, before he ever ruled anything.

teach.h: A PATRON OF LITHUANIA AND POLAND.
teach.b: He is buried in the cathedral in Vilnius, and Lithuania and Poland both claim him as a patron.

In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says on the mountain: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." Casimir was a king's son who chose to be remembered as one of those children instead.
Refusing a fight is not always the easy road. For a prince, it meant his father's anger, a lost crown, and a quiet life the court didn't understand.

how: Catholics keep 4 March as the memorial of Saint Casimir, with special celebrations in Lithuania and Poland, where pilgrims visit his chapel in Vilnius cathedral and a traditional Kaziukas fair is held in Vilnius around his feast.

games.q: you're a young prince at the head of an army, sent by your father the king to take a neighboring crown. what do you do?
o: press on and take the crown.
turn back, and refuse to march again.
send the army on without you.
games.why: Casimir turned back. his father was furious, but tradition says he would not be talked into that war again.

practice: Find one fight you're in or about to be in, an argument you're rehearsing, a group chat you're ready to win, and ask whether it's worth marching for.

If it isn't, picture yourself turning the horse around, and let it cost what it costs: being right, the last word. If you pray, ask God for the peace Jesus blesses; if you don't, breathe out slowly and set the next line down.
